q: How does the book distinguish bitcoin from Bitcoin?
options: bitcoin with a small b is the unit of currency, Bitcoin with a capital B is the system
bitcoin is the network and Bitcoin is the unit of currency
bitcoin names the whole coin, and Bitcoin names the smallest part of it that a block is able to record
The two spellings are interchangeable in the book
why: The book's tip sets the convention: the unit is bitcoin, the system is Bitcoin.

q: What does the pair BTC/USD in a price quotation name?
options: A wallet format for United States users
The currency pair whose exchange rate is being quoted
The fee rate charged by an exchange
A standard of the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals that fixes how finely a bitcoin may be divided
why: BTC is the abbreviation of the unit, so BTC/USD is the pair bitcoin against the US dollar.

q: Why is the total supply described as just below 21 million rather than exactly 21 million?
options: Because some bitcoin has been lost by its owners
Because the first block created no bitcoin at all
Because each era's subsidy is rounded down to whole satoshis
Because the cap written into the software is lowered a little at each of the halvings of the subsidy
why: Integer arithmetic on satoshis loses the fractions, so the sum falls short by 0.0231 bitcoin.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(sum((50 * 10**8 >> era) * 210000 for era in range(33)) / 10**8)
why: Summing the subsidy of all 33 paying eras in satoshis and converting gives 20999999.9769 bitcoin.

q: After how many blocks does the block subsidy halve?
why: The constant for the halving interval on the main network is 210000 blocks.

q: What does this program print?
why: Block 840000 is four halvings after the start, so 50 bitcoin shifted right four times is 3.125.

q: What does it mean that bitcoin has a floating exchange rate?
options: Its value is pegged to a fixed amount of gold
Its value is recalculated once a day by a pricing service and published for all markets
Its value against another currency moves with supply and demand in each market
Its value is the same in every market by protocol rule
why: A floating rate is not fixed by anyone; it follows the trades in the markets.

q: What does this program print?
why: At 60000 dollars per bitcoin, 0.001 bitcoin is worth 60.0 dollars.

q: Which two functions of a central bank does mining take over, according to the chapter?
options: Currency issuance and the clearing of transactions
Printing the banknotes of a country and setting the interest rate for its banks
Lending to banks and holding foreign reserves
Identity verification and fraud investigation
why: The chapter says mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions.

q: Why does the chapter call the bitcoin currency deflationary over the long term?
options: Because every halving destroys half of the existing bitcoin
Because the rate at which new bitcoin is issued keeps falling and finally stops
Because the price of bitcoin must fall as more is mined
Because the transaction fees of each block are burned rather than paid out to its miner
why: Issuance diminishes by rule, so the growth of the supply tends to zero.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import datetime
start = datetime.datetime(2009, 1, 3, 18, 15, 5)
print((start + datetime.timedelta(seconds=6_930_000 * 600)).date())
why: 6930000 blocks of 600 seconds after the first block's time falls on 2140-10-08.

q: Why is proof of work hard to produce but easy to check?
options: The hash function is secret, so only miners can compute it
Verification is carried out by a central server that keeps a list of all the answers found so far
The work is encrypted and only nodes hold the key
Finding an input whose hash has the required form needs many tries, but one hash verifies it
why: The whitepaper notes the average work is exponential in the zero bits while one hash verifies.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import hashlib
n = 0
while not hashlib.sha256(f'SEN0401-{n}'.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000'):
    n += 1
print(n)
why: The loop counts numbers until the hash of the text starts with four zeros; 15083 is the first.

q: What is the double-spend problem?
options: That two people could own the same private key
That the same unit of digital money could be spent twice
That one transaction could pay two different addresses belonging to the same person
That a miner could claim two block subsidies
why: It is the possibility of spending one unit of digital money more than once.

q: What does this program print?
code:

result = []
for coin in ('coin7', 'coin7'):
    result.append(coin not in spent)
    spent.add(coin)
print(result)
options: [True, True]
[False, False]
[True, False]
[False, True]
why: The first spend of the coin is accepted and the second is refused, because it is already in the set.

q: What is the title of the 2008 paper that first described Bitcoin?
options: Mastering Bitcoin: Programming the Open Blockchain
Hashcash: A Denial of Service Counter-Measure
The Byzantine Generals Problem
Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
why: That is the title under which Satoshi Nakamoto published the design.

q: Why is Bitcoin Core called the reference implementation?
options: It descends from the first implementation and shows how each part should be built
It is the only program that the consensus rules allow to connect to the network
It is maintained by the person who invented Bitcoin
It defines the exchange rate that wallets display
why: It grew out of Nakamoto's own software and serves as the model for the parts of the system.

q: What security disadvantage does the chapter name for desktop wallets?
options: Desktop computers cannot store private keys at all
General-purpose operating systems are often insecure and poorly configured
Desktop wallets are obliged to hand their keys over to a third-party service
Desktop wallets cannot validate transactions
why: The chapter warns that platforms such as Windows and macOS are often insecure and poorly configured.

q: Why do most mobile wallets reduce their user's privacy?
options: They publish the user's name together with each payment
They store a copy of the recovery code on the server of the phone's manufacturer
They fetch information from remote servers, disclosing addresses and balances
They sign transactions with a key shared by all users
why: To avoid storing large amounts of data they ask remote servers, which learn what they ask for.

q: What does a web wallet usually give up in exchange for ease of use?
options: The ability to receive payments at all
The ability to show a balance converted into the user's national currency
Any connection to the Bitcoin network
Control of the keys, which the third-party server holds
why: Most web wallets take control of the keys from users in exchange for ease of use.

q: What does a full node validate?
options: The entire history of Bitcoin transactions
Only the transactions of its own wallet
Only the blocks that were produced during the last day of the network
Only the signatures, not the amounts
why: The chapter defines it as a program that validates the entire history of transactions.

q: What is the other name for a lightweight client, and what does it describe?
options: Pruned node, which deletes the old blocks once it has finished checking them
Simplified-payment-verification client, which validates only partly and asks others for data
Mining client, which produces blocks for a pool
Custodial client, which holds other people's keys
why: The chapter gives SPV as the alternative name and says it validates partially.

q: What responsibility follows from using a noncustodial wallet?
options: Reporting each payment that is made to the exchange which issued the wallet
Running a full node alongside the wallet
Backing up the keys, because losing them means losing access to the bitcoin
Keeping the wallet connected to the internet at all times
why: Only the user holds the keys, so only the user can back them up.

q: What is a recovery code used for in a noncustodial wallet?
options: As the password that encrypts the wallet's connection to the nodes of the network
As the address to which other people send payments
As the fee rate the wallet will pay for a transaction
As the basis from which all the wallet's keys are generated and can be rebuilt
why: The chapter says it is used as the basis for the keys the wallet generates.

q: What does this program print?
code:
code = 'nephew dog crane clever quantum crazy purse traffic repeat fruit old clutch'
print(len(code.split()))
why: The sample recovery code of the chapter is a sentence of twelve words.

q: Where is a new Bitcoin address registered when a wallet creates it?
options: With the reference implementation's registry
Nowhere: the wallet generates it without reference to any service
With the currency exchange that sold the user their first bitcoin
In the first block that follows its creation
why: The chapter stresses that addresses are generated independently, with no registration.

q: Why can an address be shared without risking the funds behind it?
options: Because the address expires after one payment
Because the address is encrypted by the wallet before it is shared with anyone
Because spending requires the private key, and only the owner can start a spend
Because the network refuses payments from strangers
why: Unlike a bank account number, knowing an address does not let anyone withdraw.

q: What does the receiving side of a payment actually do?
options: It signs the transaction that actually moves the funds to the new owner
It chooses the fee the transaction will pay
It adds the transaction to a block
It shows an address or invoice for the sender to pay
why: Receiving shows a destination; the sender's wallet does the signing.

why: 0.001 bitcoin is 1.0 millibitcoin and 100000 satoshis.

q: What can the controller of a W3C Decentralized Identifier do without anyone's permission?
options: Change the identifier's syntax
Prove control over the identifier
Revoke another controller's identifier
Issue a national identity document
why: The specification says the design enables the controller to prove control without permission.

q: Why does the chapter call buying from a friend the least complicated method?
options: The friend is able to reverse the payment afterwards if something goes wrong
It is the only method that needs no wallet
No company, identity check or account is needed between the two people
It is the only method with no exchange rate
why: The two parties simply agree a rate and make the transfer themselves.

q: What does earning bitcoin mean in the chapter's two examples?
options: Being paid interest on a deposit of bitcoin left with a custodian
Receiving the block subsidy for mining
Winning bitcoin in a prize draw
Selling a product or service and being paid in bitcoin
why: The chapter's examples are a programmer selling skills and a hairdresser cutting hair for bitcoin.

q: What does a Bitcoin ATM do?
options: It takes cash and sends bitcoin to the user's smartphone wallet
It prints out a paper copy of the user's private key for safe keeping
It stores bitcoin on behalf of the user
It mines blocks on behalf of the user
why: The chapter defines it as a machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoin to a phone wallet.

q: What does a currency exchange provide?
options: A wallet whose keys the user holds alone
A market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin for local currency
A node that validates the whole blockchain
A published list of the improvement proposals that Bitcoin Core implements
why: The chapter describes exchanges as markets linked to a bank account.

q: In what sense is the bitcoin currency entirely virtual?
options: The coins exist as individual files that their owner keeps and stores
The coins exist only inside exchanges
There are no coins at all; the coins are implied by the transactions
The coins are backed by a reserve of gold
why: The chapter says there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins.

q: What does this program print?
why: Adding what each person received and subtracting what they sent gives Alice 70000 and Eve 35000.

q: What limits the chapter puts on the word borderless?
options: Where bitcoin meets traditional systems, national regulations still apply
Only residents of certain countries may run a node
The protocol refuses payments between different countries
Every payment must pass through a currency exchange in the sender's own country
why: The protocol knows no borders, but exchanges and banks are regulated.

q: What does decentralized by design mean for Bitcoin?
options: The software of the network is written by volunteers living in many countries
There is no central authority or point of control that could be attacked or corrupted
The blockchain is stored in several data centres
Each user may choose their own consensus rules
why: The chapter's words are: free of any central authority or point of control.

q: Against whom does the chapter say a decentralized currency must be robust?
options: Competing digital currencies only
Its own developers only
Antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements
Users of the currency who have lost their own recovery codes
why: The sidebar names both legitimate governments and criminal elements.

q: What does peer-to-peer mean for the full nodes of the network?
options: Each node is assigned a rank of its own by the reference implementation
Each node connects to exactly one other node
Only the oldest nodes may relay transactions
They can all perform the same functions and there are no special nodes
why: The network chapter says the peers can all perform the same functions, with no special nodes.

q: What does this program print?
code:
links = {'A': ['B', 'C'], 'B': ['A', 'D'], 'C': ['A', 'E'], 'D': ['B', 'F'], 'E': ['C', 'F'], 'F': ['D', 'E', 'G'], 'G': ['F']}
seen, frontier, rounds = {'A'}, {'A'}, 0
while len(seen) < len(links):
    frontier = {n for f in frontier for n in links[f]} - seen
    seen |= frontier
    rounds += 1
print(rounds)
why: Starting from A, the gossip reaches every one of the seven nodes after four rounds.

q: Why must Bitcoin's transaction journal be public?
options: Because the law requires the record to be open
Because the absence of a transaction can only be confirmed by knowing all of them
Because a record kept privately would be far too large for anyone to store
Because the miners are paid for publishing it
why: The whitepaper argues that transactions must be publicly announced for this reason.

q: What do the consensus rules cover, in the chapter's list of Bitcoin's parts?
options: The format of addresses and invoices
The fee rate that wallets should suggest
Independent transaction validation and currency issuance
The choice of the operating system on which a node is to be run
why: The third part is the set of rules for independent validation and for issuance.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def accept(claim, height, fees):
    subsidy = (50 * 10**8) >> (height // 210000)
    return claim <= subsidy + fees
print([accept(312_500_000, 840000, 0), accept(312_500_001, 840000, 0), accept(325_000_000, 840000, 12_500_000)])
options: [True, True, True]
[False, False, True]
[True, False, False]
[True, False, True]
why: A claim of exactly the subsidy passes, one satoshi more fails, and the subsidy plus fees passes.

q: Why does the chapter explain Bitcoin's monetary rules before its technical machinery?
options: Because every mechanism of the system exists to protect one of those rules
Because the monetary rules of a currency are far easier to change later than the software that enforces them
Because the price of bitcoin determines how mining works
Because a central bank publishes the rules the network follows
why: The branch is put first because each later mechanism serves a monetary rule.

q: What two things does the Unit section of the chapter fix?
options: The exchange rate against the dollar and the hours during which the market for it is open
The name of the currency and the smallest amount that can be recorded
The block interval and the difficulty of mining
The address format and the invoice format
why: The section settles the vocabulary: bitcoin and Bitcoin, and the satoshi.

q: Why does Bitcoin software count amounts in whole satoshis rather than in fractions of a bitcoin?
options: Because the satoshi is the only unit that a wallet application is permitted to display to its user
Because the protocol forbids amounts smaller than one bitcoin
Because whole numbers of the smallest unit avoid the rounding errors of fractions
Because exchanges quote their prices in satoshis
why: The smallest recordable unit is the satoshi, so amounts are integers and no fraction is lost.

q: What does this program print?
why: One bitcoin is 10**8 satoshis, so 0.001 bitcoin is 100000 of them.

q: What does the supply schedule of Bitcoin fix?
options: How much new bitcoin each block may create and therefore the total that will ever exist
How many transactions may be put into one block
How often the difficulty of mining is recalculated
How many of the nodes on the network must agree with one another before a payment counts as accepted
why: The schedule gives the subsidy per block, and the sum of all subsidies is the total supply.

q: What is the block subsidy, as distinct from the transaction fees of a block?
options: The total of the amounts that the senders of all the transactions in the block have paid
The new bitcoin that the block is allowed to create for whoever produced it
The deposit a miner must lock up before mining
The cost of the electricity used to find the block
why: The subsidy is newly created money; the fees come from the senders of the transactions.

q: What does this program print?
why: At the first block of each of the first five eras the subsidy is halved once more.

q: According to the chapter, who sets the price of bitcoin?
options: The developers who maintain the reference implementation of the protocol
The miners, through the fees they accept
An international committee of exchanges
Markets, through the trades that buyers and sellers make
why: The chapter answers the common question in one line: the price is set by markets.

q: Why does a pricing service weight each trade's price by its volume?
options: So that a large trade influences the published rate more than a small one
So that the oldest trade of the day sets the rate
So that the rate can never fall
So that every market in the world contributes exactly one price to the published figure
why: Weighting by volume makes the average represent the money actually traded.

q: What does this program print?
code:

print(sum(p * v for p, v in trades) / sum(v for p, v in trades))
why: Three units at 100 and one at 104 give (300 + 104) / 4, which is 101.0.

q: What does the chapter mean by saying that mining decentralizes currency issuance?
options: Every user may print as much bitcoin as they wish
The miners of the network vote once a year on how much new bitcoin may be created
New money is created by a rule that every participant checks instead of by one institution
An exchange issues bitcoin when a customer deposits cash
why: Issuance follows the consensus rules, which every node enforces, with no central issuer.

q: What does a central bank do that Bitcoin's rules do instead?
options: It stores the private keys of every account holder in the country it serves
It writes the software that banks run
It sets the fee for every electronic payment
It controls how much of the national currency exists
why: A central bank controls the monetary base; in Bitcoin a fixed schedule does.

q: What did earlier digital currencies use a central clearing house for?
options: To settle all transactions at regular intervals, like a traditional bank
To generate the private keys of their users
To publish the exchange rate of the currency against every other currency
To mine the new units of the currency
why: The chapter's sidebar says they cleared all transactions through a central clearinghouse.

q: Which three things is the word Bitcoin also the name of, besides the system as a whole?
options: A company, a currency and a bank
A protocol, a peer-to-peer network and a distributed computing innovation
A shared database, a web service for wallets and an operating system for nodes
A wallet, an exchange and a mining pool
why: The chapter lists exactly these three behind the scenes.

q: What does consensus mean in Bitcoin?
options: That a majority of users vote on each payment
That the developers of the reference implementation agree on the content of the next release
That the participants agree, without a leader, on one history of transactions
That every node stores the same wallet file
why: Consensus is agreement on the state of transactions reached without a central authority.

q: What does a miner actually repeat while mining?
options: A request to a central server for the next block
A fresh signature over every unconfirmed transaction waiting in the memory pool
A download of the whole blockchain
A computation over a header that refers to a list of recent transactions
why: Mining is the repeated computational task that references recent transactions.

q: What does the difficulty adjustment keep constant?
options: The number of transactions that may be placed in each block of the chain
The average time between blocks, whatever the total computing power
The subsidy that each block pays
The number of nodes on the network
why: The difficulty moves so that one block is found about every 10 minutes.

q: What does this program print?
why: Two weeks of seconds divided by a ten-minute target gives 2016 blocks per period.

q: What makes the Byzantine Generals' Problem hard?
options: The participants are too many to be counted
The messages are too large to be transmitted
The participants do not share a common language in which to describe the plan
The participants have no leader and the network may be unreliable or compromised
why: The problem is agreement without a leader over an unreliable, possibly compromised network.

q: In which years did the chapter's three landmarks of Bitcoin's history fall?
options: The paper in 2008, the network in 2009, and its author's withdrawal in 2011
The paper in 2009, the network in 2010, and the first halving in 2011
The paper in 2008, the first exchange in 2009, and the whitepaper's revision in 2012
The network in 2008, the paper in 2009, and Bitcoin Core in 2011
why: The chapter gives 2008 for the paper, 2009 for the network and April 2011 for the withdrawal.

q: What is known about Satoshi Nakamoto, according to the chapter?
options: The name belongs to a company registered in 2008
The name is an alias and the identity behind it is unknown
The person behind the name has continued to lead the project ever since it started
The name belongs to a group of university researchers
why: The chapter states that the identity of the person or people is still unknown.

q: What was Hashcash originally proposed for?
options: To issue a digital currency that was backed by a reserve of gold or a national currency
To replace passwords on web sites
To throttle systematic abuse of un-metered internet resources such as email
To compress the storage of a shared ledger
why: Back's paper gives that purpose, from which Bitcoin's proof of work descends.

q: What does this program print?

q: What weakness did the digital currencies before Bitcoin share?
options: They were centralized, so a single point could be attacked or shut down
They used no cryptography at all
They could not be exchanged for national currencies
They had no limit on how much of their money could be issued by the company behind them
why: The chapter's sidebar says they were centralized and therefore easy to attack.

q: Why does the chapter's openness group matter for a decentralized system?
options: They give one organisation the authority to approve or to reject every proposed change
Written, public documents and open code let anyone check what the rules are
They keep the protocol secret from attackers
They guarantee that every wallet behaves identically
why: Openness of documents and source is what makes the rules checkable by anyone.

q: What is a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal?
options: A vote taken among the miners of the network about a proposed change to the rules
A release of the reference implementation
A numbered design document that describes a feature or a convention
A court filing against a currency exchange
why: A BIP is a numbered design document, cited by its number.

q: What does this program print?

why: BIP 39 relates the entropy, the checksum of ENT/32 bits and the word count (ENT + CS) / 11.

q: What does the Open Source Definition require beyond access to the source code?
options: Free redistribution and permission to modify and to make derived works
A fee for commercial use of the program
Approval of each change by the original author
That the program be written in a particular programming language and build system
why: The definition opens by saying that open source is not just access to the source code.

q: What is a finished standard of the World Wide Web Consortium called?
options: A Request for Comments
A Recommendation
An Improvement Proposal
A Specification Draft
why: The consortium's finished standards carry the status Recommendation.

q: Along which three dimensions does the chapter classify wallets?
options: Purchase price, country of origin, and the programming language it is written in
Age, number of users, and licence
Platform, degree of autonomy, and who controls the keys
Block size, fee rate, and address format
why: The chapter classifies by platform, by how the wallet interacts with the network, and by key control.

q: Which four wallet platforms does the chapter list?
options: Desktop, server, mainframe and router
Full node, lightweight client, third-party interface client and miner
Custodial, noncustodial, hot and cold
Desktop, mobile, web and hardware signing device
why: Those are the four kinds in the section on the types of Bitcoin wallets.

q: Why does the chapter prefer the name hardware signing device to hardware wallet?
options: Because the device must be paired with a full-featured wallet to send and receive
Because the device cannot store private keys
Because the device is not made of hardware
Because the device holds no bitcoin of its own and cannot display a balance
why: The chapter notes the pairing requirement, and that the paired wallet's security also matters.

q: What does the second classification of wallets, by node type, actually measure?
options: How fast the wallet can display a balance
How much of the data a wallet checks for itself rather than trusting others
How many addresses the wallet can hold
Which operating system and which kind of device the wallet was written for
why: It measures the degree of autonomy: what the wallet validates and whom it depends on.

q: What must a third-party API client trust the remote system for?
options: The security of the user's private keys, but nothing else about the data
The exchange rate it displays only
Accurate information and the privacy of what it asks
Nothing, because it checks every rule itself
why: The chapter says it trusts the remote server for accurate information and for its privacy.

q: In the chapter's vocabulary, what is the difference between a peer and a client?
options: A peer is a miner and a client is a wallet
A peer is a company and a client is a private user
A peer stores the keys of its user and a client stores the blocks of the chain
A peer validates every confirmed transaction itself; a client depends on peers for valid data
why: The chapter's tip calls the full nodes the peers and the lightweight software the clients.

q: Which phrase does the chapter use to summarise the importance of key control?
options: Your keys, your coins; not your keys, not your coins
One CPU, one vote
Do not trust anybody on the network; verify everything yourself
Code is law
why: The author coined that phrase to emphasise who controls the funds.

q: What is held by somebody else when a user keeps funds with a custodian?
options: The addresses, but not the keys
The keys, and therefore the control of the funds
The recovery code, but not the keys
The record of the transaction history, though not the funds themselves
why: In a custodial arrangement the third party controls the keys and the funds on the user's behalf.

q: Why does a wallet where the user holds the keys need a backup mechanism?
options: Because the network deletes any address that has not been used for a year
Because the keys expire after a fixed period
Because nobody else can restore the keys if the device is lost
Because the exchange rate changes the keys
why: No third party holds a copy, so the user alone can provide for recovery.

q: What does the chapter say a recovery code will not restore?
options: The private keys of the wallet
The addresses the wallet had generated
The transactions recorded in the chain that the wallet had already received
The labels and other data the user entered, such as the name of each payee
why: Recovery rebuilds the onchain history but not the metadata the user added.

q: Whose story does the chapter use to show Bitcoin in use?
options: Alice, who buys her first bitcoin from her friend Joe
Satoshi Nakamoto, who mines the first block of the chain in January 2009
Bob, who runs a currency exchange
Eve, who attacks the network
why: The chapter follows Alice and Joe from the first wallet to the first confirmation.

q: What is the point of the address group of the chapter?
options: It explains how the miners of the network are paid for each block that they produce
It explains what a payee publishes, in which formats, and what that costs in privacy
It explains how a node stores the blockchain
It explains how exchanges set their prices
why: The group covers the address, the invoice and the privacy consequence of reuse.

q: What can an invoice carry that a bare address cannot?
options: The private key that is needed in order to spend the funds it points at
The fee rate that the miner must accept
An amount and a human-readable description, which the wallet can prefill
The identity of the payer
why: The chapter shows an invoice as a URI with an address, an amount and a description.

q: What can two people learn if they are both given the same address?
options: How much the other one sent to it
The private key that controls it
The name of the wallet's owner
The balance of every other address of the wallet
why: The chapter warns that two payees of one address can see each other's payments.

q: In what sense is Bitcoin's privacy pseudonymous rather than anonymous?
options: The payments themselves are hidden, while the names of the two parties are public
Payments are public but attached to addresses, which are names without a person behind them
Payments are visible only to the miner who includes them
Payments are encrypted and nobody can read them
why: The record is public; the addresses stand in for identities until one is linked to a person.

q: What does the transfer group of the chapter follow?
options: The history of the releases of the reference implementation, one by one
The path of a block from one miner to the next
A payment from the moment Send is pressed to the moment it is confirmed
The derivation of the keys from a recovery code
why: The group follows Joe's payment to Alice through its objects and stages.

q: What is a transaction, in the words of the book's glossary?
options: A request sent to a server asking it to move part of an account balance
A block of recent payments produced by a miner
An entry in a wallet's list of labels
A signed data structure expressing a transfer of value
why: The glossary defines it precisely as a signed data structure expressing a transfer of value.

q: What are the inputs and outputs of a transaction?
options: The inputs are the senders of the payment and the outputs are the miners who confirm it
The inputs name the funds being spent and the outputs assign amounts to new owners
The inputs are the fees and the outputs are the subsidies
The inputs are the addresses and the outputs are the keys
why: Inputs identify what is spent; outputs create the new spendable amounts.

q: Where does a transaction fee come from?
options: From a charge that is added by the currency exchange which sold the bitcoin
From a percentage of the block subsidy
From a deposit the receiver makes in advance
From the difference between the amounts a transaction spends and the amounts it pays out
why: The whitepaper states that the difference between input and output value is the fee.

q: Why does irreversibility make it hard to buy bitcoin with a credit card?
options: Credit card networks refuse to carry bitcoin payments
The bitcoin transaction takes considerably longer to arrive than the card payment
The seller must pay the fee of both payments
The seller cannot undo the bitcoin payment if the card payment is reversed afterwards
why: The asymmetry gives the seller the whole risk, which is why identity checks are demanded.

options: Record every payment in the public blockchain
Move value from one party to another
Require any software to be installed on the user's own device
Use Bitcoin's units of account
why: Offchain technology keeps most payments out of the public chain.

q: How many transactions does a typical payment channel add to the blockchain?
options: One for each payment
Two
None at all
Six

q: Why do companies that sell bitcoin for card payments demand identity checks?
options: Because the protocol itself requires a verified identity for every address that is used
Because the card payment can be reversed after the irreversible bitcoin has been sent
Because the miners refuse transactions from unknown senders
Because the exchange rate depends on the buyer's country
why: The check offsets the risk created by the difference in reversibility.

Because Bitcoin invented all of those ideas itself
Because chapter 1 uses technical words such as signature, key and node as if they were known

q: What is cryptography used for in Bitcoin, and what is it not used for?
options: To hide the amounts of payments from the miners
To encrypt the connection between every pair of nodes that exchange blocks
To compress the blockchain so that it fits on a phone
To prove who authorised a payment, not to hide the payments themselves
why: Bitcoin's transactions are public; the cryptography proves authorisation and protects the record.

q: What does a hash function guarantee about its output?
options: It has a fixed length and changes completely when the input changes
It can be reversed to recover the input
It is different on each occasion that the very same input is hashed again
It is shorter for shorter inputs
why: A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint, and any change to the input gives a different result.

q: What does a valid digital signature prove?
options: That the signer is a particular named person
That the data was signed at a particular time
That someone holding the private key signed exactly this data
That the person who signed intended the payment to be a fair one
why: It binds the data to the key, not to an identity or an intention.

q: What makes a pair of keys suitable for public-key cryptography?
options: The private key cannot be worked out from the public key in practice
The two keys are identical to each other but are stored in different places
Both keys must be kept secret from everyone else
The public key changes each time it is used
why: The pair is generated so that deriving the private key from the public one is infeasible.

q: Why is a Bitcoin private key chosen from an enormous range of numbers?
options: So that it can be written down in few words
So that the network can index it quickly
So that nobody can find it by trying one value after another
So that each address derived from it can be written in a shorter form
why: A 256-bit number has far too many possible values to search.

q: What does entropy measure?
options: How much uncertainty an attacker faces in guessing a secret
How long a secret is when written as words
How often a wallet generates a new address for an incoming payment
How much disk space a wallet needs
why: It is an information-theoretic measure, in bits, of the attacker's uncertainty.

q: What can a checksum do and what can it not do?
options: It corrects any single error in the data
It hides the contents of the data from anyone who happens to read it
It detects accidental changes but does not stop an attacker who recomputes it
It proves who wrote the data
why: A checksum catches mistakes; it carries no secret, so it is no defence against tampering.

q: What does mixing a secret key into a hash add?
options: Evidence that the result was produced by a holder of the key
Confidentiality of the data that was hashed
A shorter result than the hash function alone gives
A signature which anybody at all is able to verify without knowing a secret
why: A keyed hash authenticates as well as fingerprints, but only for holders of the key.

q: What does key stretching make expensive?
options: The storage of the derived key
The transmission of the key over the network
Every single guess that an attacker tries
The generation of the original entropy
why: Repeating the function many times multiplies the attacker's cost by the same factor.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import hmac
password, salt, iters = b'abandon', b'mnemonic', 2048
u = hmac.new(password, salt + bytes([0, 0, 0, 1]), 'sha512').digest()
seed = u
for _ in range(iters - 1):
    u = hmac.new(password, u, 'sha512').digest()
    seed = bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(seed, u))
print((len(seed), seed.hex()[:8]))
options: (64, 'abandon01')
why: Two thousand and forty-eight applications of HMAC-SHA512, combined with exclusive-or, give a 64-byte key beginning d96147bf.
